                                   5                                    NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   6                                            SAN JOSE DIVISION

                                   7

                                   8        FORTINET INC., et al.,                             Case No. 25-cv-09415-VKD
                                                          Plaintiffs,                          INTERIM ORDER RE PLAINTIFFS’
                                   9
                                                                                               REQUEST FOR ENTRY OF DEFAULT
                                                   v.                                          JUDGMENT BY THE CLERK OF THE
                                  10
                                                                                               COURT
                                  11        HUB CYBER SECURITY LTD.,
                                                                                               Re: Dkt. No. 31
                                                          Defendant.
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13

                                  14            Plaintiffs Fortinet International, Inc. (“Fortinet International”) and Fortinet Inc.

                                  15   (“Fortinet”) filed this breach of contract action against defendant HUB Cyber Security Ltd.

                                  16   (“HUB”). Dkt. No. 1. Defendant has not appeared in the action. Plaintiffs filed a request for

                                  17   entry of default judgment by the Clerk pursuant to Rule 55(b)(1) of the Federal Rules of Civil

                                  18   Procedure. Dkt. No. 31.

                                  19            For the reasons explained below, the Court construes plaintiffs’ request as a motion for

                                  20   default judgment by the Court pursuant to Rule 55(b)(2). The Court affords plaintiffs the

                                  21   opportunity to submit supplemental briefing in support of their motion for default judgment. If

                                  22   plaintiffs fail to submit supplemental briefing, the Court will issue an order reassigning the case to

                                  23   a district judge with a recommendation that plaintiffs’ motion for default judgment be denied

                                  24   without prejudice.

                                  25   I.       BACKGROUND
                                  26            According to the complaint, on December 28, 2015, Fortinet International entered into a

                                  27   business relationship with HUB’s subsidiary Comsec Distribution Ltd. (“Comsec”). Dkt. No. 1

                                  28   ¶¶ 7, 8. Fortinet International agreed to provide certain content security products and services, and
                                         Case 5:25-cv-09415-VKD            Document 32         Filed 07/17/26     Page 2 of 8




                                   1   Comsec agreed to market and distribute the products and services in a specific territory. Id. ¶ 15.

                                   2   In 2019, Fortinet replaced Fortinet International as the contracting party with respect to at least

                                   3   some aspects of the agreement with Comsec. Id. ¶ 26. In February 2023, HUB entered into a

                                   4   guaranty agreement with Fortinet, pursuant to which HUB guaranteed payment of the full amount

                                   5   of the invoices, plus interest, that Fortinet issued to Comsec and that Comsec failed to pay. Id.

                                   6   ¶¶ 31, 42. Fortinet alleges that Comsec has failed to pay hundreds of invoices that came due from

                                   7   February 2023 to May 2023 and owes $3,031,315.28, plus interest, attorneys’ fees and costs, to

                                   8   Fortinet. Id. ¶ 40; see also id. ¶¶ 43-426. Fortinet alleges that HUB also has failed to pay any of

                                   9   the unpaid invoices as guarantor. Id. ¶ 432.

                                  10          Plaintiffs filed this suit on October 31, 2025, asserting four claims against HUB: (1) breach

                                  11   of contract, (2) account stated, (3) unjust enrichment, and (4) open book account. Id. ¶¶ 428-449.

                                  12   Plaintiffs seek damages in the amount of $3,031,315.28, pre- and post-judgment interest,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   attorneys’ fees and costs, and costs of suit. Id. at 34-35.

                                  14          Plaintiffs represent that they served the complaint and summons on HUB on February 19,

                                  15   2026. Dkt. No. 20. On June 11, 2026, the Clerk entered default against HUB. Dkt. No. 29. On

                                  16   June 12, 2026, the Court issued an order setting July 13, 2026 as the deadline for plaintiffs’

                                  17   motion for default judgment. Dkt. No. 30. In that order, the Court advised plaintiffs that “[s]uch a

                                  18   motion must address, among other things, (1) the Court’s basis for exercising subject matter

                                  19   jurisdiction over the action and personal jurisdiction over the defendant, including service of

                                  20   process; and (2) the factors governing the appropriateness of default judgment established by the

                                  21   Ninth Circuit in Eitel v. McCool, 782 F.2d 1470, 1471-72 (9th Cir. 1986).” Id.

                                  22          On July 13, 2026, plaintiffs filed a request for entry of default judgment by the Clerk

                                  23   pursuant to Rule 55(b)(1) seeking (1) $3,031,315.28 in damages, (2) $1,809,375.98 in interest, and

                                  24   (3) $3,405 for bill of costs. Dkt. No. 31. Plaintiffs contend that because they seek “a sum certain

                                  25   due and owing to plaintiffs,” Rule 55(b)(1) applies and the Clerk may enter judgment. Id.

                                  26   II.    DISCUSSION
                                  27          A.      Sum Certain
                                  28          Plaintiffs bring their request pursuant to Rule 55(b)(1) of the Federal Rules of Civil
                                                                                          2
                                         Case 5:25-cv-09415-VKD            Document 32          Filed 07/17/26      Page 3 of 8




                                   1   Procedure, which provides that “[i]f the plaintiff’s claim is for a sum certain or a sum that can be

                                   2   made certain by computation, the [C]lerk—on the plaintiff’s request, with an affidavit showing the

                                   3   amount due—must enter judgment for that amount and costs against a defendant who has been

                                   4   defaulted for not appearing and who is neither a minor nor an incompetent person.” Fed. R. Civ.

                                   5   P. 55(b)(1). “[T]he cases discussing the sum certain requirement of Rule 55 are few and far

                                   6   between and rather exiguous in their reasoning.” Franchise Holding II, LLC. v. Huntington Rests.

                                   7   Grp., Inc., 375 F.3d 922, 928 (9th Cir. 2004) (quoting KPS & Assocs., Inc. v. Designs By FMC,

                                   8   Inc., 318 F.3d 1, 19 n.7 (1st Cir. 2003)); see also Emery G. Lee III & Jason A. Cantone, Fed. Jud.

                                   9   Ctr., Default and Default Judgment Practices in the District Courts 6-7 (March

                                  10   2024), https://www.fjc.gov/sites/default/files/materials/26/FJC_report_Rule_55_February_2024.p

                                  11   df (noting that “[c]ase law applying Rule 55(b)(1) is scarce” and “in many districts, the clerk’s

                                  12   office rarely, if ever, enters default judgments without the assigned judge’s approval, even when
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   the district does not have a local rule or policy against the clerk’s office doing so”).

                                  14           The Ninth Circuit has held that a claim is for a sum certain where “no doubt remains as to

                                  15   the amount to which a plaintiff is entitled as a result of the defendant’s default.” Franchise

                                  16   Holding, 375 F.3d at 929; see also Karen L. Stevenson & James E. Fitzgerald, Rutter Group Prac.

                                  17   Guide: Federal Civ. Proc. Before Trial (Calif. and 9th Cir. Edition) Ch. 6-D at 6:54 (Apr. 2026

                                  18   update) (noting that the “sum certain” requirement is “a high standard”). A plaintiff’s request

                                  19   meets the criteria for a sum certain, for example, where the plaintiff provides “loan documents that

                                  20   set forth the specific formulas for determining the amount owed” and “provide[s] documents

                                  21   setting forth the various amounts necessary for calculating the total amount due.” Franchise

                                  22   Holding, 375 F.3d at 929. On the other hand, inconsistencies in a plaintiff’s filings may create

                                  23   doubt sufficient to conclude that the request is not for a sum certain. See id. Similarly, claims that

                                  24   involve a party’s estimation of damages or a contract that lacks an express formula to calculate

                                  25   damages are not for a sum certain. VFS Leasing Co. v. USASIA Casino Tours/Ent., Inc., No. 14-

                                  26   cv-02941-SC, 2015 WL 82716, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 6, 2015).

                                  27           Here, it is not clear that plaintiffs’ claim is not for a sum certain. In a supporting

                                  28   declaration, plaintiffs’ representative states that plaintiffs are entitled to prejudgment interest in the
                                                                                           3
                                            Case 5:25-cv-09415-VKD        Document 32        Filed 07/17/26      Page 4 of 8




                                   1   amount of $1,809,375.98 because “[t]he interest was established at the rate of 1.5% per month, or

                                   2   18% per annum, which is the standard rate that Fortinet provides for all of its unpaid invoices and

                                   3   which Comsec and HUB agreed to . . . .” Dkt. No. 31-1 ¶ 5. However, the interest rate provision

                                   4   in the International Distributor Agreement between Fortinet and Comsec states, “Distributor shall

                                   5   pay interest on all amounts not paid when due at the rate of one and one half percent (1.5%) per

                                   6   month or the highest rate permitted by law, whichever is lower.” Id. ¶ 3, Ex. B ¶ 9.3 (emphasis

                                   7   added). Plaintiffs apply the 1.5% per month interest rate (which is the equivalent of 18% per

                                   8   annum), but their motion does not address the qualification that the interest rate provision

                                   9   contains—i.e., whether “the highest rate permitted by law” is lower than the 18% per annum rate

                                  10   plaintiffs have applied. The agreement at issue is governed by California law. See id. ¶ 3, Ex. B

                                  11   ¶ 16.2. The Court questions whether, in these circumstances, California Civil Code § 3289(b)

                                  12   supplies the correct interest rate. See Kunai, Inc. v. Allio Fintech Corp., No. 24-cv-01047-LJC,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   2024 WL 5048509, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 19, 2024) (applying 10% per annum rate pursuant to

                                  14   Cal. Civ. Code § 3289(b) where agreement provided that any overdue payments “will bear

                                  15   compound interest at the rate of the lower of (a) one and one-half percent per month; or (b) the

                                  16   highest rate permitted by applicable law”), report and recommendation adopted, No. 24-cv-

                                  17   01047-TLT, 2024 WL 5058030 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 7, 2024).

                                  18           Because plaintiffs have not established that their request for default judgment under Rule

                                  19   55(b)(1) is for a “sum certain,” the Court construes plaintiffs’ request as a motion for default

                                  20   judgment under Rule 55(b)(2). See VFS Leasing, 2015 WL 82716, at *3 (analyzing Rule 55(b)(1)

                                  21   motion for default judgment under Rule 55(b)(2) because plaintiff’s claim was not for a sum

                                  22   certain).

                                  23           B.     Jurisdiction
                                  24           When entry of judgment is sought against a party who has failed to plead or otherwise

                                  25   defend, a district court has the affirmative duty to determine whether it has jurisdiction over the

                                  26   subject matter and the parties.1 In re Tuli, 172 F.3d 707, 712 (9th Cir. 1999). Plaintiffs’ pending

                                  27
                                       1
                                  28    Courts within the Ninth Circuit have analyzed whether the court has jurisdiction over the subject
                                       matter and the parties where a plaintiff files a motion for default judgment by the Clerk pursuant
                                                                                          4
                                         Case 5:25-cv-09415-VKD             Document 32        Filed 07/17/26    Page 5 of 8




                                   1   motion for default judgment does not address the Court’s basis for exercising subject matter

                                   2   jurisdiction over the action and personal jurisdiction over the defendant, and the factual allegations

                                   3   in the complaint, even if taken as true, are insufficient.

                                   4          First, while plaintiffs invoke the Court’s diversity jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C.

                                   5   § 1332, see Dkt. No. 1 ¶ 12, plaintiffs do not affirmatively allege the citizenship of each party.

                                   6   See, e.g., Kanter v. Warner-Lambert Co., 265 F.3d 853, 857 (9th Cir. 2001) (“Absent unusual

                                   7   circumstances, a party seeking to invoke diversity jurisdiction should be able to allege

                                   8   affirmatively the actual citizenship of the relevant parties.”). The complaint alleges that “Fortinet

                                   9   is a Delaware corporation, Fortinet International is a Cayman Islands corporation, and HUB is an

                                  10   Israeli corporation.” Dkt. No. 1 ¶ 12. However, for purposes of diversity jurisdiction, “a

                                  11   corporation shall be deemed to be a citizen of every State and foreign state by which it has been

                                  12   incorporated and of the State or foreign state where it has its principal place of business.” 28
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   U.S.C. § 1332(c)(1). Plaintiffs have not identified the principal place of business for any party. In

                                  14   addition, plaintiffs have not complied with the requirement to file a disclosure statement pursuant

                                  15   to Rule 7.1 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and Civil Local Rule 3-15. See Fed. R. Civ. P.

                                  16   7.1(a)(2); Civil L.R. 3-15(b)(3).

                                  17          Second, the complaint alleges that the Court may exercise personal jurisdiction over HUB,

                                  18   a foreign defendant, because HUB operates throughout the United States and is a publicly traded

                                  19   company. Dkt. No. 1 ¶ 9. General allegations that a defendant operates throughout the country

                                  20   and is a publicly traded company are insufficient to establish personal jurisdiction over the

                                  21   defendant. See Columbia Cas. Co. v. SMI Liquidating, No. 10-cv-02057-CRB, 2010 WL

                                  22   3037242, at *3 (N.D. Cal. July 30, 2010) (allegations that defendants’ products “were used

                                  23   throughout the country” with “no supporting facts or detail” were insufficient to establish personal

                                  24   jurisdiction over defendants); Baglama v. MWV Consumer & Off. Prods., No. 12-cv-1209-

                                  25

                                  26
                                       to Rule 55(b)(1). See, e.g., VFS Leasing, 2015 WL 82716, at *2; Johnson v. Beard, No. 15-cv-
                                  27   1313-DJC-KJN P, 2023 WL 8261590, at *2 (E.D. Cal. Nov. 29, 2023), report and
                                       recommendation adopted, No. 15-cv-1313-DJC-KJNP, 2024 WL 1344849 (E.D. Cal. Mar. 29,
                                  28   2024); Allstream Bus. US, LLC v. Carrier Network Sols., LLC, No. 20-cv-01970-IM, 2021 WL
                                       3488086, at *3 (D. Or. Aug. 9, 2021).
                                                                                       5
                                         Case 5:25-cv-09415-VKD            Document 32         Filed 07/17/26      Page 6 of 8




                                   1   FMOJPRX, 2013 WL 12200647, at *5 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 19, 2013) (broad assertions that defendants

                                   2   conducted business within the district and that one defendant is a publicly traded corporation did

                                   3   not establish that defendants were subject to the court’s personal jurisdiction).

                                   4          The complaint further alleges that the Court has personal jurisdiction over HUB because

                                   5   the guaranty is governed by the laws of California; at least one of the parties to the guaranty was

                                   6   in California; and HUB agreed to perform by paying Fortinet which is headquartered in California.

                                   7   Dkt. No. 1 ¶¶ 10-11. The choice-of-law provision relied on by plaintiffs cannot, without more,

                                   8   establish personal jurisdiction over HUB. See Thayer v. Sawyer, No. 24-cv-01749-BLF, 2025 WL

                                   9   489364, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 12, 2025) (noting that while a forum selection clause may evidence

                                  10   consent to personal jurisdiction in that forum, a choice-of-law provision is not dispositive of

                                  11   whether a court can exercise personal jurisdiction over a defendant); Lazar v. Charles Schwab &

                                  12   Co., No. 12-cv-02141-BROANX, 2014 WL 12680663, at *6 (C.D. Cal. July 3, 2014) (“[T]he
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   question of whether a dispute . . . must be decided under California law is separate from the

                                  14   question of whether this Court has personal jurisdiction over [defendant].”). HUB’s contract with

                                  15   Fortinet, which plaintiffs allege is headquartered in California, is also insufficient to create

                                  16   personal jurisdiction over HUB in California. See, e.g., Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S.

                                  17   462, 478 (1985) (“If the question is whether an individual’s contract with an out-of-state party

                                  18   alone can automatically establish sufficient minimum contacts in the other party’s home forum,

                                  19   we believe the answer clearly is that it cannot.”); Boschetto v. Hansing, 539 F.3d 1011, 1017 (9th

                                  20   Cir. 2008) (“[W]e are guided by the Supreme Court’s admonition that the formation of a contract

                                  21   with a nonresident defendant is not, standing alone, sufficient to create jurisdiction.”).

                                  22          Accordingly, plaintiffs have not established the basis for the Court’s exercise of subject

                                  23   matter jurisdiction over this action or personal jurisdiction over HUB, a foreign defendant.

                                  24   Plaintiffs’ supplemental briefing should address these issues.

                                  25          C.      Arbitration Clause
                                  26          The International Distributor Agreement includes the following arbitration clause:

                                  27                  Settlement of Controversies. Any controversies or claims arising
                                                      from or relating to this Agreement, or the breach thereof, which
                                  28
                                                                                          6
                                             Case 5:25-cv-09415-VKD         Document 32         Filed 07/17/26      Page 7 of 8




                                                       cannot be amicably settled by and between the parties, shall be
                                   1                   referred to and finally settled by the rules of International Chamber
                                   2                   of Commerce, Incoterms. The place of arbitration shall be in Santa
                                                       Clara, California, United States of America. Award for such dispute
                                   3                   will be rendered by a single, neutral, mutually agreeable arbitrator.
                                                       If any action or proceeding is commenced to enforce this Agreement
                                   4                   or any right arising in connection with this Agreement, the
                                                       prevailing party in such action or proceeding shall be entitled to
                                   5
                                                       recover from the other party the reasonable attorneys fees, costs and
                                   6                   expenses incurred by such prevailing party in connection with such
                                                       action or proceeding.
                                   7

                                   8   Dkt. No. 31-1 ¶ 3, Ex. B ¶ 16.3.
                                   9            Plaintiffs do not address whether the arbitration clause applies to plaintiffs’ claims in this
                                  10   action and, if it does, whether default judgment is nevertheless appropriate. Plaintiffs’
                                  11   supplemental briefing should address this issue.
                                  12            D.     Eitel factors
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13            As noted above, the complaint asserts four different claims for relief against HUB: (1)
                                  14   breach of contract, (2) account stated, (3) unjust enrichment, and (4) open book account. Dkt. No.
                                  15   1 ¶¶ 428-449. Plaintiffs’ motion does not indicate whether plaintiffs seek default judgment as to
                                  16   all claims, or only some of them.
                                  17            Plaintiffs’ supplemental briefing must state for which claims plaintiffs seek default
                                  18   judgment and must include an analysis of the factors governing the appropriateness of default
                                  19   judgment established by the Ninth Circuit in Eitel v. McCool, 782 F.2d 1470, 1471-72 (9th Cir.
                                  20   1986).
                                  21   III.     CONCLUSION
                                  22            Plaintiffs’ supplemental briefing addressing the issues identified in this order must be filed
                                  23   by August 7, 2026. If plaintiffs fail to submit supplemental briefing that addresses these issues,
                                  24   the Court will issue an order reassigning the case to a district judge with a recommendation that
                                  25   plaintiffs’ motion for default judgment be denied without prejudice.
                                  26   //
                                  27   //
                                  28   //

                                   1          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                   2   Dated: July 17, 2026
